one_liner: SNOW-V stream cipher plus GHASH AEAD; ~13% faster than OpenSSL AES-256-GCM at 16 KB on an i7-8650U laptop.
what_it_does: SNOW-V-GCM is the AEAD mode defined in the SNOW-V paper (Ericsson/Lund, IACR ToSC 2019(3), FSE 2020), a 5G-candidate stream cipher with a 256-bit key and 128-bit IV. It keeps GCM's structure but replaces the AES-CTR keystream with SNOW-V: keystream block 0 is the GHASH key H, block 1 masks the tag, and the remaining blocks encrypt the data. It is not a library: the paper prints a portable 32-bit C/C++ reference and an AVX2/AES-NI version (SnowV256 plus snowv_gcm_encrypt/decrypt taking key32, iv16 and AAD, and appending a 16-byte tag), whose GHASH is left as an external dependency.
how_it_is_fast: SNOW-V is an LFSR plus FSM stream cipher. It uses two full AES encryption rounds (_mm_aesenc_si128 with zero round keys) as the FSM nonlinearity, keeps the two 16-bit-cell LFSRs in two 256-bit AVX2 registers so that one update does 8 LFSR steps, and outputs 128 bits of keystream per clock. On the i7-8650U that keystream alone ran at 58.25 Gbps versus 35.06 Gbps for OpenSSL AES-256-CTR asm at 16 KB. Wrapped in a PCLMULQDQ GHASH, it fell to 38.91 Gbps: the authors did not stitch GHASH into the keystream loop the way OpenSSL's AES-GCM asm does, and they say an assembly version could do better.
when_to_use: Research or interoperability work on the SNOW-V / 3GPP 256-bit algorithm candidates, where you need the published SNOW-V-GCM construction and its test vectors (Appendix C, Listing 3).
Bulk AEAD of large messages (4 KB and up) on AES-NI + AVX2 CPUs from the Skylake/Kaby Lake era without VAES, where the paper's own data shows a small edge over OpenSSL AES-256-GCM.
Platforms where AES-NI is missing: the paper argues SNOW-V stays usable with 16/32/64-bit registers while AES-256 becomes much slower, though it gives no SNOW-V-GCM numbers for that case.
As a baseline when benchmarking newer AES-round-based AEADs (Rocca, AEGIS, HiAE), which all compare against SNOW-V.
when_not_to_use: Messages of 1 KB or less: in the paper's own Table 3 OpenSSL AES-256-GCM wins at 1024 B (27.22 vs 26.16 Gbps), 256 B (17.32 vs 13.93) and 64 B (8.54 vs 5.16).

Modern CPUs with VAES/AVX-512 or Apple/AMD cores. In the authors' own SNOW-Vi paper, the SNOW-V keystream alone already loses to OpenSSL AES-256-CTR on an i7-1065G7 (58.52 vs 68.09 Gbps), a Ryzen 5 3600 (55.16 vs 68.84) and an Apple M1 (39.06 vs 58.61). HiAE's Table 10 has SNOW-V-GCM below OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM on all seven x86 CPUs it tested (e.g. 19.92 vs 51.90 Gbps on a Ryzen 9 7950X). HiAE's SNOW-V-GCM curve is nearly flat (13.04 Gbps at 16 KB vs 6.96 at 64 B on a Xeon W9-3495X), which points to a slow GHASH in that build, so that comparison probably understates the cipher.

Production code: there is no maintained open-source SNOW-V-GCM library. The one C++ library found with SNOW-V-GCM (Protocol++, jpgreninger/protocolpp) is commercially licensed, and the paper's benchmarked AVX2/PCLMULQDQ build and harness were never published.

Anything needing standards-track or FIPS-approved AEAD, nonce-misuse resistance or key commitment: it inherits every GCM restriction (unique IVs, SP 800-38D length limits) and adds SNOW-V's own limits of 2^64 keystream per key/IV and 2^64 IVs per key.

Threat models with power side channels on microcontrollers: SNOW-SCA (HOST 2024) recovers the full 256-bit SNOW-V key from an unprotected Cortex-M4 implementation with fewer than 50 traces per key byte.

integration.form: source-drop (code listings in the paper's Appendices D and E; no repository or package)
integration.dependencies: An external GHASH implementation for the SIMD version (not provided). The 32-bit reference includes a slow bit-by-bit ghash_mult marked 'Informative'.
integration.min_toolchain: Not documented. Benchmarks used Visual Studio 2017 (C++ with struct methods and templates); the SIMD listing needs a compiler with AVX2/AES-NI intrinsics such as _mm256_zextsi128_si256.
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AES-NI, SSSE3, AVX2 (plus PCLMULQDQ for a fast GHASH) for the SIMD code; the 32-bit reference is portable and endianness-free. The paper also reports an ARM NEON SNOW-V keystream (iPhone X A11) but no NEON SNOW-V-GCM.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The reference keeps all cipher state in a per-call SnowV256/SnowV32 object on the stack, with only read-only globals (S-box, constants), so separate calls share no mutable state.

gotchas: The printed SIMD snowv_gcm_decrypt calls SNOWV_ENCDEC(snowv, ciphertext + i, plaintext + i), but the macro's signature is (snowv, out, in). As printed, it writes into the ciphertext buffer instead of producing plaintext. Fix it and check against the SNOW-V-GCM test vectors before any use.

The SIMD loops load and store whole 16-byte blocks, so a message whose length is not a multiple of 16 is over-read by up to 15 bytes. The output buffer must reserve length + 16 bytes, as the listing's comments say. Decrypt also subtracts 16 from ciphertext_sz without checking its size first.

H is the first keystream block of each (key, IV) pair, not a per-key constant as in AES-GCM. Any precomputed GHASH table of H powers must therefore be rebuilt for every message, which hurts short messages (derived from the mode definition).
The 32-bit reference decrypt compares the tag with an early-exit byte loop (not constant time) and calls exit(1) on failure. The SIMD version compares with _mm_test_all_zeros instead.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over libaegis (AEGIS-128L, maintained, about 3x AES-256-GCM) or HiAE only when you specifically need SNOW-V compatibility for 3GPP-related work. On speed alone, HiAE's Table 10 puts AEGIS-128L, Rocca and HiAE roughly 4x to 21x ahead of SNOW-V-GCM at 16 KB on every CPU tested, although its ARM SNOW-V builds were SSE2NEON conversions.
verified_claims_summary: On one Intel i7-8650U laptop, single-threaded, with Visual Studio 2017 and 'most possible optimizations', the authors' C++ SNOW-V-GCM (AVX2/AES-NI/PCLMULQDQ intrinsics) reached 38.91 Gbps at 16 KB versus 34.42 Gbps for OpenSSL 3.0.0-dev (2019-04-01) AES-256-GCM asm. Both were measured with OpenSSL's own speed-loop code, reporting the best of several 1 to 3 second runs with key/IV setup per message. The curves cross near 2 KB, and AES-GCM leads below that.
status_note: A paper-only design (ePrint 2018/1143, last revised 2019-08-27, CC BY) with no maintained implementation; the authors' 2021 SNOW-Vi paper and HiAE's 2025 benchmarks both show it losing to AES on newer CPUs, so treat it as a reference, not a deployable library.
